title: Almost £1bn government cash to North West for 7,500 new homes

input.lead: The money is part of nearly £10bn announced for councils and housing associations nationally
input.summary: The money is part of nearly £10bn announced for councils and housing associations nationally
input.evidence_text: Almost £1bn government cash to North West for 7,500 new homes - BBC News Image source, EPA/Shutterstock By Hannah Richardson Local Democracy Reporting Service Published 1 hour ago The government is to give nearly £1bn to the North West to deliver about 7,500 new homes as part of plans to "build the country out of a housing crisis". A share of up to £10bn has been announced for councils and housing associations nationally in the first wave of government funding to boost "genuinely affordable homes". Greater Manchester has been given the largest share of the six mayoral areas to benefit from this round, with Liverpool City Region set to deliver 3,100 homes supported by £380m. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged the largest post-war council housebuilding programme to tackle severe shortages and homelessness, saying "no child should be raised in a hostel room". Nationally, almost 180,000 children are growing up without a permanent home, according to the government. The Prime Minister said the cash will go to regional mayors, councils, housing associations and other providers, and will be spent on building "genuinely affordable homes". Around 60% of the more than 70,000 properties are expected to be social rent. They will be in the first wave of Labour's £39bn 10-year Social and Affordable Homes Programme , external . The government said it aimed to help families "trapped in temporary accommodation or stuck on housing waiting lists' into safe, secure homes". Image caption, Liverpool City Region is set to deliver 3,100 homes Burnham said: "No child should be raised in a hostel room and no family should wait ten years for a front door of their own. title: Oldham community garden's food supply hit by dry summer

input.lead: A community garden in Oldham has lost three quarters of plants, fruit and vegetables due to hot weather
input.summary: A community garden in Oldham has lost three quarters of plants, fruit and vegetables due to hot weather
input.evidence_text: A community garden has been forced to throw away food which was destined for the local community as a result of recent dry weather Volunteers from Northern Lily Community Hub in Oldham said up to three quarters of its plants, fruit and vegetables simply did not survive the hot summer "Normally we grow over a tonne of food which equates to 12,700 meals worth and we give that away to our community," Victoria Holden from the garden said "Unfortunately, I'm not sure we'll get to a tonne this year and that's real fresh food that normally supports our community which is now not going to be available." "We lost a lot of plants. We had to just reduce everything down in the polytunnel to what could cope with that sometimes 55 degree heat," she said Holden said tropical plants like the chillies, gourds, aubergines and tomatoes had survived but the produce was "about a quarter full to where it would normally be at this stage in the year"

title: Mum says painful condition 'overlooked' during pregnancy

input.lead: Grace, 28, has spoken out about her traumatic pregnancy in the hope others do not suffer the same ordeal
input.summary: Grace, 28, has spoken out about her traumatic pregnancy in the hope others do not suffer the same ordeal
input.evidence_text: A mum who suffered from pre-eclampsia during pregnancy said she felt her symptoms were "overlooked" due to her underlying sickle cell disease Grace, 28, from Manchester, was in her second trimester when she started noticing how "physically taxing" her pregnancy had become including "extreme pain" It was only when she was admitted to St Mary's Hospital in Manchester with a sickle cell disease (SCD) unit that she was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy-related condition that can cause high blood pressure, and went on to have an emergency Caesarean She has called for urgent research and more awareness of SCD so people do not suffer the same trauma ordeal she did She said: "It's not often you get pre-eclampsia present itself and not be flagged up "It was just something that was so overlooked that any symptom that was raised or any issue that was raised, they just put it down to sickle cell."

input.summary: Jane Coates says she hopes to meet the district attorney and call for the investigation to be reopened
input.evidence_text: The mother of a British woman who was unlawfully killed after being shot by her father in Texas is preparing to travel to the US to try to persuade prosecutors to reopen the investigation into her death Lucy Harrison, 23, from Warrington, was shot in the chest on 10 January 2025 in Prosper, near Dallas Police in the town investigated her death as possible manslaughter but no criminal case was brought against her father Kris Harrison after a grand jury in Collin County declined to indict him Lucy Harrison's mother Jane Coates said she hopes to meet the district attorney and call for a fresh investigation. The Collin County District Attorney's Office has been approached for comment Harrison, a 23-year-old fashion buyer, was shot by her father at his home in Texas the day before she was due to fly home to the UK A grand jury in Collin County later decided there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges after Kris Harrison said the Glock handgun discharged accidentally while he was showing it to his daughter

They have been using their share of a £15m funding pot from Historic England, aimed at rescuing historic buildings from dereliction or demolition. Among the sites to get money were Salford Lads and Girls Club in Greater Manchester, and Morecambe's Winter Gardens. Historic England said the work to bring new life to heritage "can help build a better future for people and places". The theatre's preservation trust said that the 19th-century building had been "stabilised" by the repairs. "That sounds quite extreme, but it was a major piece of structural engineering we needed to do," said Prof Vanessa Toulmin, chair of Morecambe Winter Gardens. Image source, Morecambe Winter Gardens Image caption, Morecambe Winter Gardens had about 50 volunteers who helped with the project The theatre was opened in 1897, before closing its doors in 1977 and remaining shut for almost four decades. Toulmin said the completed work meant the theatre could continue plans to expand its capacity to more than 1,200 people. "We have around 50 volunteers who are all local, and locals make up for 50% of our visitors, which is amazing. "It just gives people in Morecambe a lot of pride, but it also ensures the building is still a place for them." title: Mum wants people to know 'there is hope after pregnancy loss'

input.lead: Hayley Metcalfe, 37, suffered the loss of two babies at 17 and 19 weeks into the pregnancies
input.summary: Hayley Metcalfe, 37, suffered the loss of two babies at 17 and 19 weeks into the pregnancies
input.evidence_text: Mum wants people to know 'there is hope after pregnancy loss' - BBC News Image source, Family handout Image caption, Hayley and Mike Metcalfe welcomed baby Hope earlier this year By Georgie Docker North West Published 24 August 2026 A woman who welcomed a daughter after two pregnancy losses has said she wants others who face similar heartache to know "there is still hope". Hayley Metcalfe, 37, from Runcorn in Cheshire, said she and her husband Mike were "over the moon" to find out she was pregnant with her second son in 2023. But what followed was three years of heartbreak when Hayley suffered a placental abruption at 19 weeks pregnant and was told her baby boy, who they had named Oscar, had died. The following year, the couple lost a second baby, who they had named Leo, at 17 weeks pregnant. "The road after baby loss is never easy and trusting again can feel impossible," said Hayley. "But I want people to know there can still be hope." Image source, Handout Image caption, Hayley and Mike Metcalfe had their youngest child Hope via C-section in February Hayley said the couple had always wanted to start a family and, in 2019, the pair welcomed their eldest son George. She recalled how she had a normal pregnancy with George so when she fell pregnant again in 2023, her and husband Mike were excited to grow their family. But at 19 weeks and four days into her pregnancy, Hayley said she felt as though "something wasn't right". An ultrasound later confirmed that Oscar had died. "It sounds awful, but when you know your baby is no longer alive, you just want it all to be over," she said. "We already had so many baby things at home. "I just couldn't bear to look at them. title: Why police are flying drones over Manchester's railway tracks

input.lead: The remotely operated aircraft can patrol lines for trespassers, reducing potential train delays
input.summary: The remotely operated aircraft can patrol lines for trespassers, reducing potential train delays
input.evidence_text: Police drones are being launched remotely over railway lines in Manchester as part of a scheme aimed at finding trespassers and reducing delays The aircraft are kept in weatherproof boxes at sites beside the railway and can be launched remotely by pilots based in London when an incident is reported Since the British Transport Police (BTP) launched its first site in Leeds in April 2025, four sites have been introduced across south London, as well as sites in Leicester and Manchester The BPT said Manchester was chosen because it is a known hotspot for trespass and disruption A pilot does not need to be on or near the site before the drone can take off, and the drone can also be used proactively - to patrol areas where intelligence suggests trespassing may be taking place BTP hopes to establish further sites in the North West as it expands the programme, although no additional locations have been announced so far

input.evidence_text: Police drones are being launched remotely over railway lines in Manchester as part of a scheme aimed at finding trespassers and reducing delays The aircraft are kept in weatherproof boxes at sites beside the railway and can be launched remotely by pilots based in London when an incident is reported Since the British Transport Police (BTP) launched its first site in Leeds in April 2025, four sites have been introduced across south London, as well as sites in Leicester and Manchester The BPT said Manchester was chosen because it is a known hotspot for trespass and disruption A pilot does not need to be on or near the site before the drone can take off, and the drone can also be used proactively - to patrol areas where intelligence suggests trespassing may be taking place BTP hopes to establish further sites in the North West as it expands the programme, although no additional locations have been announced so far

title: Council secures court order following unauthorised encampment at Oldham Edge

input.lead: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge
input.summary: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge
input.evidence_text: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge. Council officers first visited the site on Thursday 6th August following concerns from residents and people using the park. Officers spoke to those at the encampment, who said they intended to leave by Saturday 8th August. As the site had not been vacated, the Council returned with support from Greater Manchester Police on Tuesday 11th August. A formal direction was served under Section 77 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, requiring those at the encampment to leave and remove their vehicles and belongings. The Council also provided information about authorised sites in Greater Manchester, along with advice about health, wellbeing and reporting hate crime. After the direction was not followed, the Council began court proceedings. On Monday 17th August, Tameside Magistrates’ Court granted an order requiring the removal of the encampment. The site was vacated later that day. A significant amount of waste was left behind, which has now been removed by the Council’s cleansing team. A Council spokesperson said: “We understand the concerns raised by residents and people using Oldham Edge, and we thank them for their patience while we followed the legal process. “We always try to resolve unauthorised encampments through discussion and voluntary cooperation wherever possible. However, when the site was not vacated as agreed, it became necessary to take further action. “We worked closely with Greater Manchester Police throughout to make sure the situation was handled lawfully and proportionately. “The encampment has now left and our cleansing team has completed the clean-up, allowing the area to be returned to the local community.”

title: Meet the artists bringing Oldham's Town of Culture to life

input.lead: Thirteen local artists, schools, charities and community groups have been chosen to bring their ideas to life during Oldham’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture
input.summary: Thirteen local artists, schools, charities and community groups have been chosen to bring their ideas to life during Oldham’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture
input.evidence_text: Thirteen local artists, schools, charities and community groups have been chosen to bring their ideas to life during Oldham’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture. From theatre, film and music to a new mural and giant fuzzy felt artwork, the projects cover a wide range of art forms and celebrate Oldham’s people, places and stories. Oldham secured the Town of Culture title with its programme, Rising Up. Earlier this year, local creatives were invited to apply for a Town of Culture micro-commission. There were 84 applications, with 13 projects chosen to receive funding. Some of the successful artists and groups recently came together to mark the start of the programme. Not everyone was able to attend, but all 13 projects will play an important part in Oldham’s Town of Culture year. A huge Oldham welcome to: Sew Oldham – Isobel Pickup and Fay Buchanan The Oldham Panorama, a famous view of the town created in 1876, is 150 years old this year. Isobel and Fay will reimagine it for today using patchwork and running-stitch embroidery. Local people will be invited to add buildings and places that are important to them, using old clothes and fabric from home. A New Mural for Oldham – Deggy Art Deggy taught himself how to spray-paint during lockdown, starting with a painting of Joe Exotic. It snowballed from there and his murals can now be seen across Greater Manchester and Derbyshire. He will create a new mural on Oldham’s high street; the subject is a secret for now. We can’t wait to see it! Rising Faces – New Bridge School SEND Students at New Bridge School in Hollinwood will create their own faces from clay before decorating them with colour, ribbons and other materials. The faces will be brought together in an exhibition celebrating the students’ different personalities

Reports linked to the address included disorderly and intimidating behaviour, suspected drug-related activity and the order aims to provide respite to residents and protect them from disruption. Closure Orders can be obtained by councils and police where a property is linked to serious nuisance, disorder or criminal activity. The order will remain in place for three months initially. The court can extend it for a further three months if necessary, and longer-term measures may also be considered to prevent future problems and protect the local community. Residents played a vital role in securing the order by providing information and evidence about the issues affecting the area. A council spokesperson said: "This Closure Order demonstrates our commitment to protecting residents and tackling behaviour that negatively affects our communities. input.evidence_text: Events EU €3 Customs Duty Rule 2026: What This Means for UK Exporters EU €3 Customs Duty Rule 2026: What This Means for UK Exporters Official Chamber Post FREE Online Thursday 10 Sep 10am - 11am Book Now About the event The way low-value goods enter the European Union is changing From 1 July 2026, the EU introduced a new €3 customs duty on low-value consignments valued up to €150 entering the EU from outside the bloc. The change removes the previous duty exemption and introduces new considerations for businesses exporting goods directly to EU customers The new duty applies based on product categories/tariff classifications rather than simply per parcel, meaning shipments containing different types of goods could face multiple charges. For example, a parcel containing products under different tariff headings may attract multiple While the change is aimed largely at addressing the growth of low-value e-commerce imports, it will also impact UK businesses selling products directly into EU markets, including online retailers, brands and SMEs What the new €3 EU customs duty means for UK businesses
